The Weight of Small Things

I keep thinking about the way my grandmother peeled an apple—one continuous spiral, the skin curling down like a ribbon, never breaking. She did it without looking, her hands knowing the shape of the fruit better than her eyes did. I was seven. I tried to copy her and cut my thumb. She didn't flinch. She just pressed the wound to her lips, tasted the blood, and said, "Now you know where the edge is."

I don't know why I remember that. I remember other things, of course—the sound of her house settling at night, the particular silence of snow falling, the way she hummed when she thought no one was listening. But it's the apple that stays. The spiral. The blood. The lesson disguised as accident.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 3 AM. Not every night. Just enough. I've started to think of it as a kind of clock, a reminder that time passes even when I'm trying to sleep through it. The dog's name is Biscuit. I've never seen Biscuit. I know his name because my neighbor calls it out the window, apologetic, *Biscuit, come in, Biscuit, it's late, Biscuit, please*—and then the barking stops, and there's this strange intimacy to it, two people I've never met, negotiating the dark.

I used to hate it. Now I wait for it. The not-knowing of when. The small hope that tonight might be the night it doesn't come, and then the relief when it does, because at least something is predictable.

---

There's a photograph of me at twelve that I can't look at. Not because anything happened in it—I'm standing in front of a birthday cake, smiling, the whole stupid tableau—but because of what I can't see. The camera caught the moment, but not the thought behind it. I was thinking, I remember now, *this is the last time I'll be happy without knowing it.* I didn't know that then. How could I? But the photograph knows. The photograph always knows. It holds the future in its flat, chemical light, and I can't look at it without feeling like I'm cheating, like I'm reading ahead in a book I was supposed to experience slowly.

I keep it in a drawer. Not hidden. Just... set aside. Like a tool I'm not ready to use.

---

I read somewhere that octopuses have three hearts, and that two of them stop beating when they swim. The third keeps going, pumping blood through a body that's mostly arm, mostly hunger, mostly alone. They die after they mate. The males, anyway. The females guard their eggs until they hatch and then they starve, having forgotten to eat, having become something else entirely—guardian, sacrifice, the last thing standing between their children and everything that wants to eat them.

I think about this when I'm lonely. Not the romance of it. The biology. The way love can be a kind of architecture, built from need, collapsing when the need is met. The way we are all, in some way, guarding something. Waiting for something. Becoming something we weren't before we started.

---

My mother called last week. She doesn't call often. We talked about the weather, which is her code for *I don't know what else to say.* It's been eleven years since my father died, and she still sets the table for four on holidays. I used to think this was sad. Now I think it's brave. The refusal to let the dead be edited out of the story. The stubborn, aching, necessary act of continuing to set a place for someone who won't come.

I told her about the dog. She laughed. She said, "Your father used to talk to the neighbors' dogs. He'd have whole conversations with them." I didn't know this. She said it like it was obvious, like I should have known, like the dead are still here in these small details, waiting to be noticed.

---

I'm learning to cook. Not well. The way my grandmother did, with her hands knowing things. I burn garlic. I oversalt. I once made a soup so bad I ate it anyway, standing at the counter, because I couldn't bear to throw it away, because it felt like failure to waste food, even bad food, even my own bad food. The soup was gray. It tasted like regret. I ate all of it.

My grandmother would have laughed. She would have tasted it, made a face, and said, "Now you know where the heat is too high." She would have shown me. She would have let me try again.

---

There's a tree outside my window. I don't know what kind. It loses its leaves in October, all at once, like it's been holding them and finally decided to let go. I watch it every year. I've started to think of it as a kind of friend, this tree that doesn't speak, that just stands there, being a tree, surviving winters I don't understand, growing in directions I can't predict.

Last spring, a branch broke. I heard it from inside, a sound like a gunshot, and I ran outside to find it lying in the grass, still green, still full of leaves that would never fall naturally. I left it there for a week. I didn't know what to do with it. Finally, I dragged it to the curb, and the city took it away, and I felt something like grief, though I couldn't have said for what. The tree was fine. The branch was dead. But it had been part of the whole, and now it was gone, and the tree didn't seem to notice, or if it did, it didn't show it.

---

I'm afraid of becoming someone who doesn't notice. This is the fear underneath all the others. The fear of the flat life, the life of habit and convenience, where the days blur together and you wake up one morning and realize you've been sleepwalking through years you can't remember. I'm afraid of the photograph I'll find someday, the one where I'm smiling at a cake, thinking nothing, having no idea what's coming.

I'm trying to pay attention. To the dog. To the tree. To the way my mother's voice sounds when she says my name, like she's surprised I'm still here, still hers, still answering when she calls.

---

The apple spiral. I tried again last week. I cut my thumb, same place, same depth, almost. The skin curled. It broke. I ate the apple anyway, standing at the sink, bleeding into the water, watching the red swirl away.

Now I know where the edge is.
